entries.title: Mission 1: The Sublevel
entries.description: Before you judge anybody, be worth judging. Clear %OBJECTIVE_COUNT(clear_sublevel) of the infestation in MILITARY STORAGE 6, then report back to Mrs. Jones.
entries.details:
CONTACT
Mrs. Jones

REPEAT
One time

DIFFICULTY
1

OBJECTIVES
• Defeat 10 × Denizens of Very Easy Military Base dungeons
• Talk to Mrs. Jones

REWARDS
• 1,000 credits
• 1,000 experience
entries.conversation:
NPC: You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense.

NPC: You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?

Your response: Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones.

NPC: Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. Your file says you came here to hold people to a standard. Fine. Before you hold anybody to anything, I want to see you do a piece of unglamorous work that nobody will thank you for and nobody will watch. Interested?

Your response: If I must. What work?

Your response: Not right now. Another time?

Your response: I'm not interested. Leave me be.

NPC: The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25.

NPC: Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice.

Your response: I'm sure.

Your response: Actually, no. I'll hear you out.

NPC: Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good.

Your response: I have thought about it. Goodbye.

Your response: On reflection, I'll stay.

NPC: Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: The storage sublevel is crawling and the crews will not go down there. Ten of them, Military Storage 6, whatever is moving. There is no principle in it, no judgment to make, nobody to be right at. Just a dark room, and a job.

Your response: And this tells you what exactly about me?

NPC: Whether you can do the part with no audience. People who want to enforce a standard are usually in love with the part where everybody is looking. I have been at the burials of a few of those. Storage 6. Go.

NPC: Storage 6 is still crawling. There is no audience down there and the work is still the work. Go.

NPC: The bay is quiet, and you did not come back up here to tell me how it was going. Noted. Now relax, because the next one is the reason I sent for you at all.

Your response: Go on.

NPC: Article Nine of the Merc contract. A man who abandons wounded under his command forfeits everything, including the presumption that anybody will come for him. It is the oldest line we have and it is the only one this Base has never argued about. I have a signed accusation under it on my desk. Come back when you are ready, and we will talk about what that costs.

NPC: Are you ready?

Your response: Tell me about the accusation.

Your response: Give me a minute.

NPC: Take it. Take two.

NPC: Sergeant Dain Vos. Wastes patrol, three weeks ago, contact at the ridge. Two of his people went down alive. He stripped their ammunition and their medkits and he walked, and he has been drinking in Sector 1 ever since, telling anybody who asks that they were already gone. Yeah, they were not. One of them lasted six hours.

Your response: Who signed the accusation?

NPC: A quartermaster's man who was on the ridge with them. It is witnessed, it is filed, and the provosts have already found the ammunition in Vos's locker with two other people's marks on it. Article Nine does not go to a court, recruit. It goes to whoever the Base sends. Today that is you. Sector 1, the bar next to the Gene Replicator. He will know why you are there.

NPC: I know why you're here. You have the walk. Three weeks I have been in this bar every day, waiting for somebody with that walk.

Your response: The ridge. Two of your people were alive when you left them.

NPC: ...Yes. They were. I'm not gonna even try to tell you that they weren't. You have the report and I've had weeks to get tired of lying about it to myself and everyone else. Kell lasted six hours. I have thought about that every night since.

Your response: Then you know how this ends.

NPC: I've known since the ridge. Just one thing, and then you can get on with it: who signed the paper? Actually, no, do not tell me. Just do me one last favor. Look at his crate manifests for spring. All four months of them. I wasn't reported because of Kell.

Your response: Article Nine, Sergeant. Stand up.

NPC: It is a good article. It is the only one worth keeping. Just- make sure it stays worth keeping.

NPC: ...

NPC: Vos is in the bar next to the Gene Replicator in Sector 1 and Article Nine does not expire. Go.

NPC: It's done. Did he give you anything before the end?

Your response: He did not argue about the ridge. He wanted to know who signed the paper, and said that if it was who he thought, I should look at that man's crate manifests for spring.

NPC: ...Come again? Because I have just pulled those manifests, and there are four months of them signed by our witness, and every one has a hole in it about the size of what a man could carry out of an armory. Vos was guilty. But he knew about those holes. He is still guilty. And the mouth that told us so was buying itself an afternoon where nobody was looking. Come back when you have decided how you feel about that, and be honest about it.

NPC: Well? Have you decided how you feel?

Your response: I did the right thing for a reason that was somebody else's. That is not the same as being used, but it is close enough to anger me.

Your response: Give me a moment.

NPC: Take it. I have been sitting with the same question since last night.

NPC: Close enough is right. Here is what I want done with it, and it is not another execution. Chaplain Reyn took that accusation and passed it to me. He vouched for the witness personally. He has known the man for years, and he did not test one word of it, because he did not think he had to.

Your response: You want me to put that to a chaplain.

NPC: I want you to make him look at it, because he is the man this Base takes its conscience from and he handed me a true thing from a rotten mouth without checking which was which. Sector 1. He is expecting somebody. He is not expecting it to be the one who carried out the sentence.

NPC: She sent you. I assumed she would send somebody. I did not assume it would be the hand that did it, which I suppose is her way of making a point about consequences.

Your response: You vouched for the witness. Personally.

NPC: I did. Years and years I have known that man. He came to me on the ridge night with his hands shaking and I did not test a single word, because a man does not shake like that over a lie. That is what I told myself and it is what I told her.

Your response: He was shaking because he had months of manifests with holes in them.

NPC: ...I have read them. She sent them across last night and I have read them four times looking for another explanation, which is exactly the sin I am guilty of in the first place. Looking for the answer that I wanted to be true.

Your response: Vos was still guilty. The article still held.

NPC: It held this time. That is the whole horror of it, and I want you to hear me say it out loud because I will not be trusted to say it again for a while. If I will pass an untested accusation when it happens to be true, then I will pass one when it is not. The article will do exactly what it did this week, and a man will die correctly for the wrong reason. The code is not what protects us. Testing it is.

Your response: Then say that to the provosts, not to me.

NPC: I am saying it to them at first watch, with my name on it and all the facts, so nobody has to dig for them. Go and tell her. And- thank you for coming yourself. It would have been easier from anybody else, and I do not wish this to be easy.

NPC: First watch. My name at the top. Go on.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1 and he is waiting for somebody. Go and let it be you.

NPC: Reyn has put his name on an appointment in front of the provosts. How did he take it?

Your response: Badly, and then properly. He said the code is not what protects us. Testing it is.

NPC: Testing it is, all too true. He is a better man than he gives himself credit for. The witness is with the provosts, the manifests are open, and Article Nine survives with one more line under it about where accusations have to come from.

Your response: And Vos is still dead.

NPC: Vos is still dead and Vos was still guilty, and you are going to have to carry both of those at once for the rest of your career, because that is what this work actually is. You do not get certainty, just the carrying.

Your response: Then what do I hold on to?

NPC: This. A true thing from a rotten mouth is still true, and it still has to be tested, because the mouth will lie to you the very next time and you will have taught yourself not to check. Test the accusation, always, even when you would very much like to get on with it. There is an attack module coming your way for the work, so keep training that Aggressive PSI Use and stay somebody who can be argued with. And do yourself a favor: the mission terminals here at the Base always need the wastes thinned out. Steady work keeps a runner sharp. Dismissed. Welcome to the Mercs.

entries.title: Mission 2: Article Nine
entries.description: Sgt. Dain Vos stripped his own wounded and ran. He is drinking in the bar next to the Gene Replicator in MILITARY BASE SEC-1. Carry out the sentence, then report back to Mrs. Jones.
entries.details:
CONTACT
Mrs. Jones

REPEAT
One time

DIFFICULTY
1

POSSIBLE PREREQUISITES
• Complete Mission 1: The Sublevel
Other conditions may also apply.

OBJECTIVES
• Defeat Sgt. Dain Vos
• Talk to Mrs. Jones

REWARDS
• 2,000 credits
• 2,000 experience
entries.conversation:
NPC: You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense.

NPC: You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?

Your response: Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones.

NPC: Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. Your file says you came here to hold people to a standard. Fine. Before you hold anybody to anything, I want to see you do a piece of unglamorous work that nobody will thank you for and nobody will watch. Interested?

Your response: If I must. What work?

Your response: Not right now. Another time?

Your response: I'm not interested. Leave me be.

NPC: The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25.

NPC: Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice.

Your response: I'm sure.

Your response: Actually, no. I'll hear you out.

NPC: Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good.

Your response: I have thought about it. Goodbye.

Your response: On reflection, I'll stay.

NPC: Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: The storage sublevel is crawling and the crews will not go down there. Ten of them, Military Storage 6, whatever is moving. There is no principle in it, no judgment to make, nobody to be right at. Just a dark room, and a job.

Your response: And this tells you what exactly about me?

NPC: Whether you can do the part with no audience. People who want to enforce a standard are usually in love with the part where everybody is looking. I have been at the burials of a few of those. Storage 6. Go.

NPC: Storage 6 is still crawling. There is no audience down there and the work is still the work. Go.

NPC: The bay is quiet, and you did not come back up here to tell me how it was going. Noted. Now relax, because the next one is the reason I sent for you at all.

Your response: Go on.

NPC: Article Nine of the Merc contract. A man who abandons wounded under his command forfeits everything, including the presumption that anybody will come for him. It is the oldest line we have and it is the only one this Base has never argued about. I have a signed accusation under it on my desk. Come back when you are ready, and we will talk about what that costs.

NPC: Are you ready?

Your response: Tell me about the accusation.

Your response: Give me a minute.

NPC: Take it. Take two.

NPC: Sergeant Dain Vos. Wastes patrol, three weeks ago, contact at the ridge. Two of his people went down alive. He stripped their ammunition and their medkits and he walked, and he has been drinking in Sector 1 ever since, telling anybody who asks that they were already gone. Yeah, they were not. One of them lasted six hours.

Your response: Who signed the accusation?

NPC: A quartermaster's man who was on the ridge with them. It is witnessed, it is filed, and the provosts have already found the ammunition in Vos's locker with two other people's marks on it. Article Nine does not go to a court, recruit. It goes to whoever the Base sends. Today that is you. Sector 1, the bar next to the Gene Replicator. He will know why you are there.

NPC: I know why you're here. You have the walk. Three weeks I have been in this bar every day, waiting for somebody with that walk.

Your response: The ridge. Two of your people were alive when you left them.

NPC: ...Yes. They were. I'm not gonna even try to tell you that they weren't. You have the report and I've had weeks to get tired of lying about it to myself and everyone else. Kell lasted six hours. I have thought about that every night since.

Your response: Then you know how this ends.

NPC: I've known since the ridge. Just one thing, and then you can get on with it: who signed the paper? Actually, no, do not tell me. Just do me one last favor. Look at his crate manifests for spring. All four months of them. I wasn't reported because of Kell.

Your response: Article Nine, Sergeant. Stand up.

NPC: It is a good article. It is the only one worth keeping. Just- make sure it stays worth keeping.

NPC: ...

NPC: Vos is in the bar next to the Gene Replicator in Sector 1 and Article Nine does not expire. Go.

NPC: It's done. Did he give you anything before the end?

Your response: He did not argue about the ridge. He wanted to know who signed the paper, and said that if it was who he thought, I should look at that man's crate manifests for spring.

NPC: ...Come again? Because I have just pulled those manifests, and there are four months of them signed by our witness, and every one has a hole in it about the size of what a man could carry out of an armory. Vos was guilty. But he knew about those holes. He is still guilty. And the mouth that told us so was buying itself an afternoon where nobody was looking. Come back when you have decided how you feel about that, and be honest about it.

NPC: Well? Have you decided how you feel?

Your response: I did the right thing for a reason that was somebody else's. That is not the same as being used, but it is close enough to anger me.

Your response: Give me a moment.

NPC: Take it. I have been sitting with the same question since last night.

NPC: Close enough is right. Here is what I want done with it, and it is not another execution. Chaplain Reyn took that accusation and passed it to me. He vouched for the witness personally. He has known the man for years, and he did not test one word of it, because he did not think he had to.

Your response: You want me to put that to a chaplain.

NPC: I want you to make him look at it, because he is the man this Base takes its conscience from and he handed me a true thing from a rotten mouth without checking which was which. Sector 1. He is expecting somebody. He is not expecting it to be the one who carried out the sentence.

NPC: She sent you. I assumed she would send somebody. I did not assume it would be the hand that did it, which I suppose is her way of making a point about consequences.

Your response: You vouched for the witness. Personally.

NPC: I did. Years and years I have known that man. He came to me on the ridge night with his hands shaking and I did not test a single word, because a man does not shake like that over a lie. That is what I told myself and it is what I told her.

Your response: He was shaking because he had months of manifests with holes in them.

NPC: ...I have read them. She sent them across last night and I have read them four times looking for another explanation, which is exactly the sin I am guilty of in the first place. Looking for the answer that I wanted to be true.

Your response: Vos was still guilty. The article still held.

NPC: It held this time. That is the whole horror of it, and I want you to hear me say it out loud because I will not be trusted to say it again for a while. If I will pass an untested accusation when it happens to be true, then I will pass one when it is not. The article will do exactly what it did this week, and a man will die correctly for the wrong reason. The code is not what protects us. Testing it is.

Your response: Then say that to the provosts, not to me.

NPC: I am saying it to them at first watch, with my name on it and all the facts, so nobody has to dig for them. Go and tell her. And- thank you for coming yourself. It would have been easier from anybody else, and I do not wish this to be easy.

NPC: First watch. My name at the top. Go on.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1 and he is waiting for somebody. Go and let it be you.

NPC: Reyn has put his name on an appointment in front of the provosts. How did he take it?

Your response: Badly, and then properly. He said the code is not what protects us. Testing it is.

NPC: Testing it is, all too true. He is a better man than he gives himself credit for. The witness is with the provosts, the manifests are open, and Article Nine survives with one more line under it about where accusations have to come from.

Your response: And Vos is still dead.

NPC: Vos is still dead and Vos was still guilty, and you are going to have to carry both of those at once for the rest of your career, because that is what this work actually is. You do not get certainty, just the carrying.

Your response: Then what do I hold on to?

Test the accusation, always, even when you would very much like to get on with it. There is an attack module coming your way for the work, so keep training that Aggressive PSI Use and stay somebody who can be argued with. And do yourself a favor: the mission terminals here at the Base always need the wastes thinned out. Steady work keeps a runner sharp. Dismissed. Welcome to the Mercs.

entries.title: Mission 3: Who Accuses
entries.description: The man who reported Vos had his own reasons. Put it to Chaplain Reyn in MILITARY BASE SEC-1, then report back to Mrs. Jones.
entries.details:
CONTACT
Mrs. Jones

REPEAT
One time

DIFFICULTY
1

POSSIBLE PREREQUISITES
• Complete Mission 2: Article Nine
Other conditions may also apply.

OBJECTIVES
• Talk to Chaplain Reyn
• Talk to Mrs. Jones

REWARDS
• 3,000 credits
• 3,000 experience
entries.conversation:
NPC: You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense.

NPC: You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?

Your response: Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones.

NPC: Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. Your file says you came here to hold people to a standard. Fine. Before you hold anybody to anything, I want to see you do a piece of unglamorous work that nobody will thank you for and nobody will watch. Interested?

Your response: If I must. What work?

Your response: Not right now. Another time?

Your response: I'm not interested. Leave me be.

NPC: The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25.

NPC: Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice.

Your response: I'm sure.

Your response: Actually, no. I'll hear you out.

NPC: Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good.

Your response: I have thought about it. Goodbye.

Your response: On reflection, I'll stay.

NPC: Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: The storage sublevel is crawling and the crews will not go down there. Ten of them, Military Storage 6, whatever is moving. There is no principle in it, no judgment to make, nobody to be right at. Just a dark room, and a job.

Your response: And this tells you what exactly about me?

NPC: Whether you can do the part with no audience. People who want to enforce a standard are usually in love with the part where everybody is looking. I have been at the burials of a few of those. Storage 6. Go.

NPC: Storage 6 is still crawling. There is no audience down there and the work is still the work. Go.

NPC: The bay is quiet, and you did not come back up here to tell me how it was going. Noted. Now relax, because the next one is the reason I sent for you at all.

Your response: Go on.

NPC: Article Nine of the Merc contract. A man who abandons wounded under his command forfeits everything, including the presumption that anybody will come for him. It is the oldest line we have and it is the only one this Base has never argued about. I have a signed accusation under it on my desk. Come back when you are ready, and we will talk about what that costs.

NPC: Are you ready?

Your response: Tell me about the accusation.

Your response: Give me a minute.

NPC: Take it. Take two.

NPC: Sergeant Dain Vos. Wastes patrol, three weeks ago, contact at the ridge. Two of his people went down alive. He stripped their ammunition and their medkits and he walked, and he has been drinking in Sector 1 ever since, telling anybody who asks that they were already gone. Yeah, they were not. One of them lasted six hours.

Your response: Who signed the accusation?

NPC: A quartermaster's man who was on the ridge with them. It is witnessed, it is filed, and the provosts have already found the ammunition in Vos's locker with two other people's marks on it. Article Nine does not go to a court, recruit. It goes to whoever the Base sends. Today that is you. Sector 1, the bar next to the Gene Replicator. He will know why you are there.

NPC: I know why you're here. You have the walk. Three weeks I have been in this bar every day, waiting for somebody with that walk.

Your response: The ridge. Two of your people were alive when you left them.

NPC: ...Yes. They were. I'm not gonna even try to tell you that they weren't. You have the report and I've had weeks to get tired of lying about it to myself and everyone else. Kell lasted six hours. I have thought about that every night since.

Your response: Then you know how this ends.

NPC: I've known since the ridge. Just one thing, and then you can get on with it: who signed the paper? Actually, no, do not tell me. Just do me one last favor. Look at his crate manifests for spring. All four months of them. I wasn't reported because of Kell.

Your response: Article Nine, Sergeant. Stand up.

NPC: It is a good article. It is the only one worth keeping. Just- make sure it stays worth keeping.

NPC: ...

NPC: Vos is in the bar next to the Gene Replicator in Sector 1 and Article Nine does not expire. Go.

NPC: It's done. Did he give you anything before the end?

Your response: He did not argue about the ridge. He wanted to know who signed the paper, and said that if it was who he thought, I should look at that man's crate manifests for spring.

NPC: ...Come again? Because I have just pulled those manifests, and there are four months of them signed by our witness, and every one has a hole in it about the size of what a man could carry out of an armory. Vos was guilty. But he knew about those holes. He is still guilty. And the mouth that told us so was buying itself an afternoon where nobody was looking. Come back when you have decided how you feel about that, and be honest about it.

NPC: Well? Have you decided how you feel?

Your response: I did the right thing for a reason that was somebody else's. That is not the same as being used, but it is close enough to anger me.

Your response: Give me a moment.

NPC: Take it. I have been sitting with the same question since last night.

Your response: You vouched for the witness. Personally.

NPC: I did. Years and years I have known that man. He came to me on the ridge night with his hands shaking and I did not test a single word, because a man does not shake like that over a lie. That is what I told myself and it is what I told her.

Your response: Badly, and then properly. He said the code is not what protects us. Testing it is.

NPC: Testing it is, all too true. He is a better man than he gives himself credit for. The witness is with the provosts, the manifests are open, and Article Nine survives with one more line under it about where accusations have to come from.

Your response: And Vos is still dead.

NPC: Vos is still dead and Vos was still guilty, and you are going to have to carry both of those at once for the rest of your career, because that is what this work actually is. You do not get certainty, just the carrying.

 338        say:

 340        resume_at: jones_m3_return
 341  
 342      reyn_greeting:
 343        say:
 344          - "She sent you. I assumed she would send somebody. I did not assume it would be the hand that did it, which I suppose is her way of making a point about consequences."
 345        answer:

 347            - "You vouched for the witness. Personally."
 348  
 349      reyn_vouched:
 350        say:
 351          - "I did. Years and years I have known that man. He came to me on the ridge night with his hands shaking and I did not test a single word, because a man does not shake like that over a lie. That is what I told myself and it is what I told her."

If I will pass an untested accusation when it happens to be true, then I will pass one when it is not. The article will do exactly what it did this week, and a man will die correctly for the wrong reason. The code is not what protects us. Testing it is."

 374          - "I am saying it to them at first watch, with my name on it and all the facts, so nobody has to dig for them. Go and tell her. And- thank you for coming yourself. It would have been easier from anybody else, and I do not wish this to be easy."

entries.title: Mission 1: The Congregation
entries.description: Mrs. Jones wants you to understand what the Mercs actually believe in. Find Chaplain Reyn in MILITARY BASE SEC-1 and listen.
entries.details:
CONTACT
Mrs. Jones

REPEAT
One time

DIFFICULTY
1

OBJECTIVES
• Talk to Chaplain Reyn
• Talk to Mrs. Jones

REWARDS
• 1,000 credits
• 1,000 experience
entries.conversation:
NPC: You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense.

NPC: You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?

Your response: Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones.

NPC: Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. You have come to a mercenary base to talk to people about their souls. That is either very brave, or a filing error. I will assume brave. Before I let you say one word to my runners, you are going to sit with the man who already has that job. Interested?

Your response: Oh yes. Who is he?

Your response: Not right now. Another time?

Your response: I'm not interested. Leave me be.

NPC: The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25.

NPC: Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice.

Your response: I'm sure.

Your response: Actually, no. I'll hear you out.

NPC: Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good.

Your response: I have thought about it. Goodbye.

Your response: On reflection, I'll stay.

NPC: Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Chaplain Reyn. Sector 1. He has buried more Mercs than you have met and he has never once told any of them that it was all for some greater good or something. So go and ask him what this Base actually believes in. Do not argue with the answer, even though you might want to.

Your response: Why would I want to?

NPC: Because it is not what they taught you it should be. Because you will think that this cannot possibly be it. And because you are young enough to think that is a problem. Sector 1. Sit down and listen to the whole thing. Go.

NPC: Ah. Get comfortable. Jones only sends people to me for one of two reasons, and you do not look bereaved.

Your response: She wants me to ask you what this Base actually believes in.

NPC: Yeah, that's the other one. Everybody expects a long answer and it is a short one. Each other. That's it. That is the whole creed of the City Mercs, and I have yet to find the bottom of it.

Your response: But that's not faith. That's just a working relationship.

NPC: I could imagine that this answer is not to your liking. Let me tell you what I have learned burying people out here: faith is not what a runner thinks about on a good day. It is who they will go back into a burning room for when there is no possible profit in it. I have watched men who couldn't even name a scripture or an ethical code, but who would go back into that burning room three times for their comrades. I have also buried a man who could recite the whole liturgy and left two people on a ridge.

Your response: So what is there for me to do here?

NPC: You disappoint me. Faith gives you wings, no matter if your faith is with some deity, or just with one another. These people do the most extraordinary things for each other, and nobody ever tells them so. They go out into the wastes believing they are only worth their contract rate. You do not need to bring them any enlightenment. You need to be able to sustain their trust in one another.

Your response: Jones said I would want to argue with all this.

NPC: And you did. You complained that this would not be faith. You heard me, but you haven't understood what I'm telling you, yet. You will, in about a year. Go on. And when she gets to the part about the gate - and she will - come back to me before you do anything clever.

NPC: We have each other. That is all of it. Go on.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1 and he has all the time in the world. That is rather his condition. Go.

NPC: What does this Base believe in?

Your response: Each other, and nothing above that. He said faith out here is not what a runner thinks on a good day, it is who they will go back into a burning room for.

NPC: Oh yes. Hold on to that, because a man at my gate is currently offering my runners something much better than that, and eleven of them have taken him up on it. Get some rest. Then we are going to talk about him.

NPC: Ready to hear about the competition?

Your response: Who is at the gate?

Your response: Give me a minute.

NPC: Take it. He preaches every evening, so we know exactly where he will be.

NPC: He calls himself Brother Ossian. For weeks, every evening, he has been telling tired runners at the Military Entrance that the wastes are cleaner than the City and that there is a place out past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract. Unfortunately, he is a good speaker. He is a very good speaker.

Your response: And eleven went with him. Where are they?

NPC: That's the thing. Nine are dead. Two came back and will not say what happened to the others, which tells me most of it. There is no shangrila past the ridge, recruit. There is a man who needs an audience, and a wasteland that eats whoever he sends into it. He preaches at the gate tonight. Stop him.

NPC: Come closer, friend, you are just in time. I was telling good people about a place past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract and nothing is owed.

Your response: Just in time, eh? You can say that again. Nine of the eleven you sent out there are dead.

NPC: Dead? No no! They arrived, that is the whole- the two who came back were not ready, that is all, the wastes test whether you are ready and some people are not, but the nine, the nine got through-

Your response: How do you know? Have you ever walked out there yourself?

NPC: I do not need to walk it. I have seen it. I have seen it every night for months, and it is more real to me than this Base. And if you had seen it you would not be standing there with that face on you.

Your response: You have sent nine people to die on a thing you have never once gone to look at yourself.

NPC: ...You are trying to make me small. Everyone tries to make me small. They stood there, and listened, and they were happy for the first time in years. And you want to take that away from me, and instead give them- what? A contract? A rate? You disgust me!

NPC: ...

NPC: Ossian preaches at the Military Entrance every evening. Go.

NPC: So tell me just one thing. Did he believe any of it?

Your response: All of it. That was the worst part. He was not selling anything, he genuinely thought the nine had made it, because he never once walked out there himself.

NPC: I can't say that I'm surprised. They usually do, but it never makes the dead any less dead. But here's the kicker, the part nobody warned me about the first time I did this: his congregation is still standing at that gate. Thirty-odd runners who were promised something, and tonight there is nobody there to say something to them. A silence like that gets filled, recruit. Always. Come back when you are ready.

NPC: About thirty runners are looking forward to some sermon tonight. Ready?

Your response: What do you mean? What am I supposed to say to them?

Your response: Give me a moment.

NPC: Do not be long, lest we just have to deal with the next wannabe messiah.

NPC: No. No no, calm down. Not even I would expect that of you right now. That is why you are going back to Reyn instead of to the soapbox. He knows how to deal with this situation. He will know the words.

Your response: Didn't he just lose them, when they turned to that Ossian fellow?

NPC: I didn't say that he wouldn't learn something tonight as well. Sector 1. Go and ask him what he wishes he had said instead of what he did say.

NPC: I heard about Ossian before you got here. And thirty of them still standing there this evening with nothing to look at. You came back before you did anything clever. Good.

Your response: You have stood in front of those stares before.

NPC: And I failed every single time. The first time, I climbed straight up, and I told them the man had been a liar and they were fools for listening: I was right on both counts, and I lost every one of them. The rest was just variations on a theme. Being right at people who have just been made stupid is the fastest way to make them somebody else's.

Your response: So what will you say?

NPC: Me? Nothing. If that is the question you carried all the way here, it is the wrong one. Ossian gave them a mythical paradise some days past the ridge. You do not beat that with a reminder to trust one another. You beat it by pointing at something in this Base that is much more real than some imaginary paradise that might or might not be there. And then you get out of the way.

Your response: Point at what, then?

NPC: Do you remember what I told you the first time you came to me? Men who couldn't even name a scripture, going back into a burning room three times for their comrades. I was not being poetic. I was referring to Kettel, the man I saw perform that feat of will in Bay Nine.

Your response: Kettel? The quartermaster's engineer, down in HQ?

NPC: The very same. And in all that time not one person on this Base has asked him about it. Not one, myself included, and I have thought about it most weeks. You will be the first. Go and ask him. Then ask him to stand in front of those people tonight, and to tell them what happened, in his own flat unbearable way. Let thirty runners work out for themselves if some mythical shangrila is worth giving up their mates.

Your response: And if he says no?

NPC: Oh, he will say no. He said no to the citation, he said no to the transfer, and he will say no to you. Do not argue him out of it. He is not refusing because he is modest, but because he thinks this doesn't count. Find out why he thinks that, and then tell him the truth about it. That is the entire job.

Your response: Why would he think it does not count?

NPC: Because of who he brought out on the third trip. Ask him. That's not my story. Go on.

NPC: Ask him yourself about Bay Nine.

NPC: If this is about those spillages again, I have filed the report and I am not filing another one.

Your response: It is not. Reyn sent me. I want to ask you about Bay Nine.

NPC: ...No. No, you do not. That case is closed, and I have no use for it open. Whatever Jones is running, run it somewhere else.

Your response: Nobody has asked you. I checked. I am asking.

NPC: Because there is nothing to ask. The feed went up, the bay filled with smoke, I went in. That is not a story, that is a Tuesday with a worse outcome. People do it every week out here and nobody puts anybody on a plinth for it.

Your response: You went in three times.

NPC: Yes. Because I got it wrong twice. I came out with Ravi, and then I came out with that Odell boy, and then I stood in this corridor doing the math like an idiot and worked out that I had left Sarnow, and by then it had been four minutes, and I went back anyway.

Your response: And?

NPC: And I brought him out. And he died on the floor eleven minutes later with me pumping his chest. So you can see why I do not tell it. It is not a story about a man who saved somebody. It is a story about a man who was too slow twice and then carried a body up a stairwell so it would not be by itself.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

Your response: You saved two men. That counts whether you like it or not.

NPC: There it is. Everybody arrives there eventually and it is always in that tone, the one that has already decided what I am permitted to think about my own night. Two men. I can count. I was there for the counting.

Your response: That was the wrong thing to say. Let me try again.

NPC: Heh. Sure. Try. I have got until the shift change.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

NPC: Go on, then. Which part does matter?

Your response: Sarnow was not by himself. You knew he was probably already gone, the math told you to stay out. And yet, you went in for a man who could not pay you and could not thank you. That is the only thing anybody on this Base actually believes in. You have spent quite some time now filing it as just a... a failed repair.

NPC: ...

Your response: And now, thirty runners are waiting for the next sermon, because that liar, Ossian, told them there's an easy way out. That may even be the truth, but they were told by the wrong man. I would rather they got the proper truth, from you.

NPC: Eff that. I'm not a speaker. I am not a well-spoken man.

Your response: Good. Ossian said everything well. Just tell them about the four minutes.

NPC: ...Right. I will stand next to Reyn, I will talk about the four minutes, and nothing else. And if anybody claps, I'm leaving. And- listen. All that time, and you are the first one who asked. I want you to know that I appreciate it.

NPC: The four minutes. Nothing else.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1. Go and ask him.

NPC: Reyn gave you a name and the name is upstairs in the CityMercs HQ. Go and ask him. Asking is the whole of it.

NPC: Reyn tells me that an engineer who has not volunteered for anything in two years will be his speaker tonight. What did you say to him?

Your response: Nothing he didn't already know. I told him the four minutes counted, and I asked. Reyn says nobody had ever asked him.

NPC: You asked. That's all you had to do, and it is going to fix more than any sermon would have. Do you understand what you avoided?

Your response: Reyn told me to point at something more real, and then just get out of the way.

NPC: Then he has told you the whole job, and I don't have to pretend I am adding anything. I will say only this: I have had four preachers at this Base recently, and the three who left all left the same way. They started saying the true thing, it went well, and then they started enjoying standing on the soapbox much more than speaking the truth.

Your response: How do I know if that happens to me?

NPC: You will not, which is why you keep Reyn at the back of the room and Kettel at the front of it. When somebody hands you silence, do not fill it with yourself. Find the person in that room who has already answered it with their life, and make them heard. There are two PSI modules coming your way for this, so keep training that PSI Use, and keep somebody around who is allowed to call you an idiot. And do yourself a favor: the mission terminals here at the Base always need the wastes thinned out. Steady work keeps a runner sharp. Dismissed. Welcome to the Mercs.

entries.title: Mission 2: The Voice At The Gate
entries.description: Brother Ossian is walking runners out of this Base and into the wastes. Stop him at the MILITARY ENTRANCE, then report back to Mrs. Jones.

OBJECTIVES

REWARDS
• 2,000 credits
• 2,000 experience

You do not beat that with a reminder to trust one another. You beat it by pointing at something in this Base that is much more real than some imaginary paradise that might or might not be there. And then you get out of the way.

Your response: Point at what, then?

NPC: Do you remember what I told you the first time you came to me? Men who couldn't even name a scripture, going back into a burning room three times for their comrades. I was not being poetic. I was referring to Kettel, the man I saw perform that feat of will in Bay Nine.

Your response: Kettel? The quartermaster's engineer, down in HQ?

NPC: The very same. And in all that time not one person on this Base has asked him about it. Not one, myself included, and I have thought about it most weeks. You will be the first. Go and ask him. Then ask him to stand in front of those people tonight, and to tell them what happened, in his own flat unbearable way. Let thirty runners work out for themselves if some mythical shangrila is worth giving up their mates.

Your response: And if he says no?

NPC: Oh, he will say no. He said no to the citation, he said no to the transfer, and he will say no to you. Do not argue him out of it. He is not refusing because he is modest, but because he thinks this doesn't count. Find out why he thinks that, and then tell him the truth about it. That is the entire job.

Your response: Why would he think it does not count?

NPC: Because of who he brought out on the third trip. Ask him. That's not my story. Go on.

NPC: Ask him yourself about Bay Nine.

NPC: If this is about those spillages again, I have filed the report and I am not filing another one.

Your response: It is not. Reyn sent me. I want to ask you about Bay Nine.

NPC: ...No. No, you do not. That case is closed, and I have no use for it open. Whatever Jones is running, run it somewhere else.

Your response: Nobody has asked you. I checked. I am asking.

NPC: Because there is nothing to ask. The feed went up, the bay filled with smoke, I went in. That is not a story, that is a Tuesday with a worse outcome. People do it every week out here and nobody puts anybody on a plinth for it.

Your response: You went in three times.

NPC: Yes. Because I got it wrong twice. I came out with Ravi, and then I came out with that Odell boy, and then I stood in this corridor doing the math like an idiot and worked out that I had left Sarnow, and by then it had been four minutes, and I went back anyway.

Your response: And?

NPC: And I brought him out. And he died on the floor eleven minutes later with me pumping his chest. So you can see why I do not tell it. It is not a story about a man who saved somebody. It is a story about a man who was too slow twice and then carried a body up a stairwell so it would not be by itself.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

Your response: You saved two men. That counts whether you like it or not.

NPC: There it is. Everybody arrives there eventually and it is always in that tone, the one that has already decided what I am permitted to think about my own night. Two men. I can count. I was there for the counting.

Your response: That was the wrong thing to say. Let me try again.

NPC: Heh. Sure. Try. I have got until the shift change.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

NPC: Go on, then. Which part does matter?

Your response: Sarnow was not by himself. You knew he was probably already gone, the math told you to stay out. And yet, you went in for a man who could not pay you and could not thank you. That is the only thing anybody on this Base actually believes in. You have spent quite some time now filing it as just a... a failed repair.

NPC: ...

Your response: And now, thirty runners are waiting for the next sermon, because that liar, Ossian, told them there's an easy way out. That may even be the truth, but they were told by the wrong man. I would rather they got the proper truth, from you.

NPC: Eff that. I'm not a speaker. I am not a well-spoken man.

Your response: Good. Ossian said everything well. Just tell them about the four minutes.

NPC: ...Right. I will stand next to Reyn, I will talk about the four minutes, and nothing else. And if anybody claps, I'm leaving. And- listen. All that time, and you are the first one who asked. I want you to know that I appreciate it.

NPC: The four minutes. Nothing else.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1. Go and ask him.

NPC: Reyn gave you a name and the name is upstairs in the CityMercs HQ. Go and ask him. Asking is the whole of it.

NPC: Reyn tells me that an engineer who has not volunteered for anything in two years will be his speaker tonight. What did you say to him?

Your response: Nothing he didn't already know. I told him the four minutes counted, and I asked. Reyn says nobody had ever asked him.

NPC: You asked. That's all you had to do, and it is going to fix more than any sermon would have. Do you understand what you avoided?

Your response: Reyn told me to point at something more real, and then just get out of the way.

NPC: Then he has told you the whole job, and I don't have to pretend I am adding anything. I will say only this: I have had four preachers at this Base recently, and the three who left all left the same way. They started saying the true thing, it went well, and then they started enjoying standing on the soapbox much more than speaking the truth.

Your response: How do I know if that happens to me?

NPC: You will not, which is why you keep Reyn at the back of the room and Kettel at the front of it. When somebody hands you silence, do not fill it with yourself. Find the person in that room who has already answered it with their life, and make them heard. There are two PSI modules coming your way for this, so keep training that PSI Use, and keep somebody around who is allowed to call you an idiot. And do yourself a favor: the mission terminals here at the Base always need the wastes thinned out. Steady work keeps a runner sharp. Dismissed. Welcome to the Mercs.

 131      jones_not_available:
 132        say:
 133          - "You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense."
 134  
 135      jones_over_qualified:
 136        say:
 137          - "You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?"
 138        answer:
 139          jones_leave_over_qualified:
 140            - "Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones."
 141  
 142      jones_leave_over_qualified:
 143        do:
 144          - set_flag:
 145              flag: mb_preacher
 146              value: 3
 147          - remove
 148        say:
 149          - "Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there."
 150  
 151      jones_m1_offer:
 152        say:
 153          - "Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. You have come to a mercenary base to talk to people about their souls. That is either very brave, or a filing error. I will assume brave. Before I let you say one word to my runners, you are going to sit with the man who already has that job. Interested?"
 154        answer:
 155          jones_m1_briefing:
 156            - "Oh yes. Who is he?"
 157          jones_m1_later:
 158            - "Not right now. Another time?"
 159          jones_dismiss:
 160            - "I'm not interested. Leave me be."
 161  
 162      jones_m1_later:
 163        say:
 164          - "The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25."
 165  
 166      jones_dismiss:
 167        say:
 168          - "Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice."
 169        answer:
 170          jones_dismiss_confirm:
 171            - "I'm sure."
 172          start:
 173            - "Actually, no. I'll hear you out."
 174  
 175      jones_dismiss_confirm:
 176        say:
 177          - "Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good."
 178        answer:
 179          jones_leave:
 180            - "I have thought about it. Goodbye."
 181          start:
 182            - "On reflection, I'll stay."
 183  
 184      jones_leave:
 185        do:
 186          - set_flag:
 187              flag: mb_preacher
 188              value: 3
 189          - remove
 190        say:
 191          - "Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there."
 192  
 193      jones_m1_briefing:
 194        say:
 195          - "Chaplain Reyn. Sector 1. He has buried more Mercs than you have met and he has never once told any of them that it was all for some greater good or something. So go and ask him what this Base actually believes in. Do not argue with the answer, even though you might want to."
 196        answer:
 197          jones_m1_go:
 198            - "Why would I want to?"
 199  
 200      jones_m1_go:
 201        do:
 202          - offer_mission: mb_preacher.mission1
 203        say:
 204          - "Because it is not what they taught you it should be. Because you will think that this cannot possibly be it. And because you are young enough to think that is a problem. Sector 1. Sit down and listen to the whole thing. Go."
 205        resume_at: jones_m1_return
 206  
 207      reyn_greeting:
 208        say:
 209          - "Ah. Get comfortable. Jones only sends people to me for one of two reasons, and you do not look bereaved."
 210        answer:
 211          reyn_each_other:
 212            - "She wants me to ask you what this Base actually believes in."
 213  
 214      reyn_each_other:
 215        say:
 216          - "Yeah, that's the other one. Everybody expects a long answer and it is a short one. Each other. That's it. That is the whole creed of the City Mercs, and I have yet to find the bottom of it."
 217        answer:
 218          reyn_burning_room:
 219            - "But that's not faith. That's just a working relationship."
 220  
 221      reyn_burning_room:
 222        say:
 223          - "I could imagine that this answer is not to your liking. Let me tell you what I have learned burying people out here: faith is not what a runner thinks about on a good day. It is who they will go back into a burning room for when there is no possible profit in it. I have watched men who couldn't even name a scripture or an ethical code, but who would go back into that burning room three times for their comrades. I have also buried a man who could recite the whole liturgy and left two people on a ridge."
 224        answer:
 225          reyn_wings:
 226            - "So what is there for me to do here?"
 227  
 228      reyn_wings:
 229        say:
 230          - "You disappoint me. Faith gives you wings, no matter if your faith is with some deity, or just with one another. These people do the most extraordinary things for each other, and nobody ever tells them so. They go out into the wastes believing they are only worth their contract rate. You do not need to bring them any enlightenment. You need to be able to sustain their trust in one another."
 231        answer:
 232          reyn_you_argued:
 233            - "Jones said I would want to argue with all this."
 234  
 235      reyn_you_argued:
 236        do:
 237          - complete_objective: listen_to_reyn
 238        say:
 239          - "And you did. You complained that this would not be faith. You heard me, but you haven't understood what I'm telling you, yet. You will, in about a year. Go on. And when she gets to the part about the gate - and she will - come back to me before you do anything clever."
 240        resume_at: reyn_creed_told
 241  
 242      reyn_creed_told:
 243        say:
 244          - "We have each other. That is all of it. Go on."
 245  
 246      jones_m1_return:
 247        do:
 248          - goto: jones_m1_report
 249            when:
 250              objective_done:
 251                objective: listen_to_reyn
 252          - goto: jones_m1_not_done
 253  
 254      jones_m1_not_done:
 255        say:
 256          - "Reyn is in Sector 1 and he has all the time in the world. That is rather his condition. Go."
 257        resume_at: jones_m1_return
 258  
 259      jones_m1_report:
 260        say:
 261          - "What does this Base believe in?"
 262        answer:
 263          jones_m1_done:
 264            - "Each other, and nothing above that. He said faith out here is not what a runner thinks on a good day, it is who they will go back into a burning room for."
 265        resume_at: jones_m1_done
 266  
 267      jones_m1_done:
 268        do:
 269          - set_flag:
 270              flag: mb_preacher
 271              value: 1
 272          - complete_objective: report
 273        say:
 274          - "Oh yes. Hold on to that, because a man at my gate is currently offering my runners something much better than that, and eleven of them have taken him up on it. Get some rest. Then we are going to talk about him."
 275  
 276      jones_m2_offer:
 277        say:
 278          - "Ready to hear about the competition?"
 279        answer:
 280          jones_m2_briefing:
 281            - "Who is at the gate?"
 282          jones_m2_later:
 283            - "Give me a minute."
 284  
 285      jones_m2_later:
 286        say:
 287          - "Take it. He preaches every evening, so we know exactly where he will be."
 288  
 289      jones_m2_briefing:
 290        say:
 291          - "He calls himself Brother Ossian. For weeks, every evening, he has been telling tired runners at the Military Entrance that the wastes are cleaner than the City and that there is a place out past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract. Unfortunately, he is a good speaker. He is a very good speaker."
 292        answer:
 293          jones_m2_go:
 294            - "And eleven went with him. Where are they?"
 295  
 296      jones_m2_go:
 297        do:
 298          - offer_mission: mb_preacher.mission2
 299        say:
 300          - "That's the thing. Nine are dead. Two came back and will not say what happened to the others, which tells me most of it. There is no shangrila past the ridge, recruit. There is a man who needs an audience, and a wasteland that eats whoever he sends into it. He preaches at the gate tonight. Stop him."
 301        resume_at: jones_m2_return
 302  
 303      ossian_greeting:
 304        say:
 305          - "Come closer, friend, you are just in time. I was telling good people about a place past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract and nothing is owed."
 306        answer:
 307          ossian_they_arrived:
 308            - "Just in time, eh? You can say that again. Nine of the eleven you sent out there are dead."
 309  
 310      ossian_they_arrived:
 311        say:
 312          - "Dead? No no! They arrived, that is the whole- the two who came back were not ready, that is all, the wastes test whether you are ready and some people are not, but the nine, the nine got through-"
 313        answer:
 314          ossian_seen_it:
 315            - "How do you know? Have you ever walked out there yourself?"
 316  
 317      ossian_seen_it:
 318        say:
 319          - "I do not need to walk it. I have seen it. I have seen it every night for months, and it is more real to me than this Base. And if you had seen it you would not be standing there with that face on you."
 320        answer:
 321          ossian_attack:
 322            - "You have sent nine people to die on a thing you have never once gone to look at yourself."
 323  
 324      ossian_attack:
 325        do:
 326          - attack
 327        say:
 328          - "...You are trying to make me small. Everyone tries to make me small. They stood there, and listened, and they were happy for the first time in years. And you want to take that away from me, and instead give them- what? A contract? A rate? You disgust me!"
 329        resume_at: ossian_silent
 330  
 331      ossian_silent:
 332        say:
 333          - "..."
 334  
 335      jones_m2_return:
 336        do:
 337          - goto: jones_m2_report
 338            when:
 339              objective_done:
 340                objective: silence_ossian
 341          - goto: jones_m2_not_done
 342  
 343      jones_m2_not_done:
 344        say:
 345          - "Ossian preaches at the Military Entrance every evening. Go."
 346        resume_at: jones_m2_return
 347  
 348      jones_m2_report:
 349        say:
 350          - "So tell me just one thing. Did he believe any of it?"
 351        answer:
 352          jones_m2_done:
 353            - "All of it. That was the worst part. He was not selling anything, he genuinely thought the nine had made it, because he never once walked out there himself."
 354        resume_at: jones_m2_done
 355  
 356      jones_m2_done:
 357        do:
 358          - set_flag:
 359              flag: mb_preacher
 360              value: 2
 361          - complete_objective: report
 362        say:
 363          - "I can't say that I'm surprised. They usually do, but it never makes the dead any less dead. But here's the kicker, the part nobody warned me about the first time I did this: his congregation is still standing at that gate. Thirty-odd runners who were promised something, and tonight there is nobody there to say something to them. A silence like that gets filled, recruit. Always. Come back when you are ready."
 364  
 365      jones_m3_offer:
 366        say:
 367          - "About thirty runners are looking forward to some sermon tonight. Ready?"
 368        answer:
 369          jones_m3_briefing:
 370            - "What do you mean? What am I supposed to say to them?"
 371          jones_m3_later:
 372            - "Give me a moment."
 373  
 374      jones_m3_later:
 375        say:
 376          - "Do not be long, lest we just have to deal with the next wannabe messiah."
 377  
 378      jones_m3_briefing:
 379        say:
 380          - "No. No no, calm down. Not even I would expect that of you right now. That is why you are going back to Reyn instead of to the soapbox. He knows how to deal with this situation. He will know the words."
 381        answer:
 382          jones_m3_go:
 383            - "Didn't he just lose them, when they turned to that Ossian fellow?"
 384  
 385      jones_m3_go:
 386        do:
 387          - offer_mission: mb_preacher.mission3
 388        say:
 389          - "I didn't say that he wouldn't learn something tonight as well. Sector 1. Go and ask him what he wishes he had said instead of what he did say."
 390        resume_at: jones_m3_return
 391  
 392      reyn_heard_about_ossian:
 393        say:
 394          - "I heard about Ossian before you got here. And thirty of them still standing there this evening with nothing to look at. You came back before you did anything clever. Good."
 395        answer:
 396          reyn_failed_every_time:
 397            - "You have stood in front of those stares before."
 398  
 399      reyn_failed_every_time:
 400        say:
 401          - "And I failed every single time. The first time, I climbed straight up, and I told them the man had been a liar and they were fools for listening: I was right on both counts, and I lost every one of them. The rest was just variations on a theme. Being right at people who have just been made stupid is the fastest way to make them somebody else's."
 402        answer:
 403          reyn_point_at_something:
 404            - "So what will you say?"
 405  
 406      reyn_point_at_something:
 407        say:
 408          - "Me? Nothing. If that is the question you carried all the way here, it is the wrong one. Ossian gave them a mythical paradise some days past the ridge. You do not beat that with a reminder to trust one another. You beat it by pointing at something in this Base that is much more real than some imaginary paradise that might or might not be there. And then you get out of the way."
 409        answer:
 410          reyn_bay_nine:
 411            - "Point at what, then?"
 412  
 413      reyn_bay_nine:
 414        say:
 415          - "Do you remember what I told you the first time you came to me? Men who couldn't even name a scripture, going back into a burning room three times for their comrades. I was not being poetic. I was referring to Kettel, the man I saw perform that feat of will in Bay Nine."
 416        answer:
 417          reyn_ask_kettel:
 418            - "Kettel? The quartermaster's engineer, down in HQ?"
 419  
 420      reyn_ask_kettel:
 421        say:
 422          - "The very same. And in all that time not one person on this Base has asked him about it. Not one, myself included, and I have thought about it most weeks. You will be the first. Go and ask him. Then ask him to stand in front of those people tonight, and to tell them what happened, in his own flat unbearable way. Let thirty runners work out for themselves if some mythical shangrila is worth giving up their mates."
 423        answer:
 424          reyn_he_will_say_no:
 425            - "And if he says no?"
 426  
 427      reyn_he_will_say_no:
 428        say:
 429          - "Oh, he will say no. He said no to the citation, he said no to the transfer, and he will say no to you. Do not argue him out of it. He is not refusing because he is modest, but because he thinks this doesn't count. Find out why he thinks that, and then tell him the truth about it. That is the entire job."
 430        answer:
 431          reyn_third_trip:
 432            - "Why would he think it does not count?"
 433  
 434      reyn_third_trip:
 435        do:
 436          - complete_objective: return_to_reyn
 437        say:
 438          - "Because of who he brought out on the third trip. Ask him. That's not my story. Go on."
 439        resume_at: reyn_name_given
 440  
 441      reyn_name_given:
 442        say:
 443          - "Ask him yourself about Bay Nine."
 444  
 445      kettel_greeting:
 446        say:
 447          - "If this is about those spillages again, I have filed the report and I am not filing another one."
 448        answer:
 449          kettel_case_closed:
 450            - "It is not. Reyn sent me. I want to ask you about Bay Nine."
 451  
 452      kettel_case_closed:
 453        say:
 454          - "...No. No, you do not. That case is closed, and I have no use for it open. Whatever Jones is running, run it somewhere else."
 455        answer:
 456          kettel_nothing_to_ask:
 457            - "Nobody has asked you. I checked. I am asking."
 458  
 459      kettel_nothing_to_ask:
 460        say:
 461          - "Because there is nothing to ask. The feed went up, the bay filled with smoke, I went in. That is not a story, that is a Tuesday with a worse outcome. People do it every week out here and nobody puts anybody on a plinth for it."
 462        answer:
 463          kettel_wrong_twice:
 464            - "You went in three times."
 465  
 466      kettel_wrong_twice:
 467        say:
 468          - "Yes. Because I got it wrong twice. I came out with Ravi, and then I came out with that Odell boy, and then I stood in this corridor doing the math like an idiot and worked out that I had left Sarnow, and by then it had been four minutes, and I went back anyway."
 469        answer:
 470          kettel_sarnow:
 471            - "And?"
 472

entries.title: Mission 3: What You Say Next
entries.description: Ossian's congregation is still standing at the gate with nobody to listen to. Go back to Chaplain Reyn in MILITARY BASE SEC-1. He will give you a name: the quartermaster's engineer Kettel, at the CITYMERCS HQ. Ask Kettel yourself, then report back to Mrs. Jones.
entries.details:
CONTACT
Mrs. Jones

REPEAT
One time

DIFFICULTY
1

POSSIBLE PREREQUISITES
• Complete Mission 2: The Voice At The Gate
Other conditions may also apply.

OBJECTIVES
• Talk to Chaplain Reyn
• Talk to Kettel
• Talk to Mrs. Jones

REWARDS
• 3,000 credits
• 3,000 experience
entries.conversation:
NPC: You are not the kind of specialist I am looking for. No offense.

NPC: You are past the point where I can teach you anything, recruit. You made rank without me. Go find a war worth your time. Shall I clear out of your quarters?

Your response: Yes. Thanks anyway, Jones.

NPC: Fair enough. I will not waste a veteran's floor space. The Base mission terminals will keep you busy - steady work keeps a runner sharp. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Ah, there you are. Allow me to introduce myself: Jones, at your service. Well, not really. You have come to a mercenary base to talk to people about their souls. That is either very brave, or a filing error. I will assume brave. Before I let you say one word to my runners, you are going to sit with the man who already has that job. Interested?

Your response: Oh yes. Who is he?

Your response: Not right now. Another time?

Your response: I'm not interested. Leave me be.

NPC: The offer stands. Find me before you outrank it: I do not recruit past level /25.

NPC: Sure about that? I do not make the offer twice.

Your response: I'm sure.

Your response: Actually, no. I'll hear you out.

NPC: Think carefully. Walk away now and that frequency goes cold for good.

Your response: I have thought about it. Goodbye.

Your response: On reflection, I'll stay.

NPC: Your call. The Mercs know where to find talent when it grows up. Watch yourself out there.

NPC: Chaplain Reyn. Sector 1. He has buried more Mercs than you have met and he has never once told any of them that it was all for some greater good or something. So go and ask him what this Base actually believes in. Do not argue with the answer, even though you might want to.

Your response: Why would I want to?

NPC: Because it is not what they taught you it should be. Because you will think that this cannot possibly be it. And because you are young enough to think that is a problem. Sector 1. Sit down and listen to the whole thing. Go.

NPC: Ah. Get comfortable. Jones only sends people to me for one of two reasons, and you do not look bereaved.

Your response: She wants me to ask you what this Base actually believes in.

NPC: Yeah, that's the other one. Everybody expects a long answer and it is a short one. Each other. That's it. That is the whole creed of the City Mercs, and I have yet to find the bottom of it.

Your response: But that's not faith. That's just a working relationship.

NPC: I could imagine that this answer is not to your liking. Let me tell you what I have learned burying people out here: faith is not what a runner thinks about on a good day. It is who they will go back into a burning room for when there is no possible profit in it. I have watched men who couldn't even name a scripture or an ethical code, but who would go back into that burning room three times for their comrades. I have also buried a man who could recite the whole liturgy and left two people on a ridge.

Your response: So what is there for me to do here?

NPC: You disappoint me. Faith gives you wings, no matter if your faith is with some deity, or just with one another. These people do the most extraordinary things for each other, and nobody ever tells them so. They go out into the wastes believing they are only worth their contract rate. You do not need to bring them any enlightenment. You need to be able to sustain their trust in one another.

Your response: Jones said I would want to argue with all this.

NPC: And you did. You complained that this would not be faith. You heard me, but you haven't understood what I'm telling you, yet. You will, in about a year. Go on. And when she gets to the part about the gate - and she will - come back to me before you do anything clever.

NPC: We have each other. That is all of it. Go on.

NPC: Reyn is in Sector 1 and he has all the time in the world. That is rather his condition. Go.

NPC: What does this Base believe in?

Your response: Each other, and nothing above that. He said faith out here is not what a runner thinks on a good day, it is who they will go back into a burning room for.

NPC: Oh yes. Hold on to that, because a man at my gate is currently offering my runners something much better than that, and eleven of them have taken him up on it. Get some rest. Then we are going to talk about him.

NPC: Ready to hear about the competition?

Your response: Who is at the gate?

Your response: Give me a minute.

NPC: Take it. He preaches every evening, so we know exactly where he will be.

NPC: He calls himself Brother Ossian. For weeks, every evening, he has been telling tired runners at the Military Entrance that the wastes are cleaner than the City and that there is a place out past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract. Unfortunately, he is a good speaker. He is a very good speaker.

Your response: And eleven went with him. Where are they?

NPC: That's the thing. Nine are dead. Two came back and will not say what happened to the others, which tells me most of it. There is no shangrila past the ridge, recruit. There is a man who needs an audience, and a wasteland that eats whoever he sends into it. He preaches at the gate tonight. Stop him.

NPC: Come closer, friend, you are just in time. I was telling good people about a place past the ridge where nobody is anybody's contract and nothing is owed.

Your response: Just in time, eh? You can say that again. Nine of the eleven you sent out there are dead.

NPC: Dead? No no! They arrived, that is the whole- the two who came back were not ready, that is all, the wastes test whether you are ready and some people are not, but the nine, the nine got through-

Your response: How do you know? Have you ever walked out there yourself?

NPC: I do not need to walk it. I have seen it. I have seen it every night for months, and it is more real to me than this Base. And if you had seen it you would not be standing there with that face on you.

Your response: You have sent nine people to die on a thing you have never once gone to look at yourself.

NPC: ...You are trying to make me small. Everyone tries to make me small. They stood there, and listened, and they were happy for the first time in years. And you want to take that away from me, and instead give them- what? A contract? A rate? You disgust me!

NPC: ...

NPC: Ossian preaches at the Military Entrance every evening. Go.

NPC: So tell me just one thing. Did he believe any of it?

Your response: All of it. That was the worst part. He was not selling anything, he genuinely thought the nine had made it, because he never once walked out there himself.

NPC: I can't say that I'm surprised. They usually do, but it never makes the dead any less dead. But here's the kicker, the part nobody warned me about the first time I did this: his congregation is still standing at that gate. Thirty-odd runners who were promised something, and tonight there is nobody there to say something to them. A silence like that gets filled, recruit. Always. Come back when you are ready.

NPC: About thirty runners are looking forward to some sermon tonight. Ready?

Your response: What do you mean? What am I supposed to say to them?

Your response: Give me a moment.

NPC: Do not be long, lest we just have to deal with the next wannabe messiah.

NPC: No. No no, calm down. Not even I would expect that of you right now. That is why you are going back to Reyn instead of to the soapbox. He knows how to deal with this situation. He will know the words.

Your response: Didn't he just lose them, when they turned to that Ossian fellow?

NPC: I didn't say that he wouldn't learn something tonight as well. Sector 1. Go and ask him what he wishes he had said instead of what he did say.

NPC: I heard about Ossian before you got here. And thirty of them still standing there this evening with nothing to look at. You came back before you did anything clever. Good.

Your response: You have stood in front of those stares before.

NPC: And I failed every single time. The first time, I climbed straight up, and I told them the man had been a liar and they were fools for listening: I was right on both counts, and I lost every one of them. The rest was just variations on a theme. Being right at people who have just been made stupid is the fastest way to make them somebody else's.

Your response: So what will you say?

NPC: Me? Nothing. If that is the question you carried all the way here, it is the wrong one. Ossian gave them a mythical paradise some days past the ridge. You do not beat that with a reminder to trust one another. You beat it by pointing at something in this Base that is much more real than some imaginary paradise that might or might not be there. And then you get out of the way.

Your response: Point at what, then?

NPC: Do you remember what I told you the first time you came to me? Men who couldn't even name a scripture, going back into a burning room three times for their comrades. I was not being poetic. I was referring to Kettel, the man I saw perform that feat of will in Bay Nine.

Your response: Kettel? The quartermaster's engineer, down in HQ?

NPC: The very same. And in all that time not one person on this Base has asked him about it. Not one, myself included, and I have thought about it most weeks. You will be the first. Go and ask him. Then ask him to stand in front of those people tonight, and to tell them what happened, in his own flat unbearable way. Let thirty runners work out for themselves if some mythical shangrila is worth giving up their mates.

Your response: And if he says no?

NPC: Oh, he will say no. He said no to the citation, he said no to the transfer, and he will say no to you. Do not argue him out of it. He is not refusing because he is modest, but because he thinks this doesn't count. Find out why he thinks that, and then tell him the truth about it. That is the entire job.

Your response: Why would he think it does not count?

NPC: Because of who he brought out on the third trip. Ask him. That's not my story. Go on.

NPC: Ask him yourself about Bay Nine.

NPC: If this is about those spillages again, I have filed the report and I am not filing another one.

Your response: It is not. Reyn sent me. I want to ask you about Bay Nine.

NPC: ...No. No, you do not. That case is closed, and I have no use for it open. Whatever Jones is running, run it somewhere else.

Your response: Nobody has asked you. I checked. I am asking.

NPC: Because there is nothing to ask. The feed went up, the bay filled with smoke, I went in. That is not a story, that is a Tuesday with a worse outcome. People do it every week out here and nobody puts anybody on a plinth for it.

Your response: You went in three times.

NPC: Yes. Because I got it wrong twice. I came out with Ravi, and then I came out with that Odell boy, and then I stood in this corridor doing the math like an idiot and worked out that I had left Sarnow, and by then it had been four minutes, and I went back anyway.

Your response: And?

NPC: And I brought him out. And he died on the floor eleven minutes later with me pumping his chest. So you can see why I do not tell it. It is not a story about a man who saved somebody. It is a story about a man who was too slow twice and then carried a body up a stairwell so it would not be by itself.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

Your response: You saved two men. That counts whether you like it or not.

NPC: There it is. Everybody arrives there eventually and it is always in that tone, the one that has already decided what I am permitted to think about my own night. Two men. I can count. I was there for the counting.

Your response: That was the wrong thing to say. Let me try again.

NPC: Heh. Sure. Try. I have got until the shift change.

Your response: You are wrong about which part matters.

NPC: Go on, then. Which part does matter?

That is the only thing anybody on this Base actually believes in. You have spent quite some time now filing it as just a... a failed repair.

NPC: ...Right. I will stand next to Reyn, I will talk about the four minutes, and nothing else. And if anybody claps, I'm leaving. And- listen. All that time, and you are the first one who asked. I want you to know that I appreciate it.

NPC: The four minutes. Nothing else.

NPC: Reyn gave you a name and the name is upstairs in the CityMercs HQ. Go and ask him. Asking is the whole of it.

NPC: Reyn tells me that an engineer who has not volunteered for anything in two years will be his speaker tonight. What did you say to him?

NPC: Then he has told you the whole job, and I don't have to pretend I am adding anything.  207      reyn_greeting:

 213  
 214      reyn_each_other:
 215        say:
 216          - "Yeah, that's the other one. Everybody expects a long answer and it is a short one. Each other. That's it. That is the whole creed of the City Mercs, and I have yet to find the bottom of it."
 217        answer:
 218          reyn_burning_room:
 219            - "But that's not faith. That's just a working relationship."

 222        say:
 223          - "I could imagine that this answer is not to your liking. Let me tell you what I have learned burying people out here: faith is not what a runner thinks about on a good day. It is who they will go back into a burning room for when there is no possible profit in it. I have watched men who couldn't even name a scripture or an ethical code, but who would go back into that burning room three times for their comrades. I have also buried a man who could recite the whole liturgy and left two people on a ridge."

 225          reyn_wings:
 226            - "So what is there for me to do here?"
